title: Venus steals the geology spotlight again. This time with huge rifts that formed not long ago
summary: A study by ETH Zurich, published in Nature Geoscience, finds that enormous rift valleys on Venus may be far younger and possibly still active. Using 3D thermomechanical models, researchers examined Ganis Chasma, Dali Chasma and Davana Chasma and estimated crustal spreading of about 3–10 cm per year, likely driven by mantle plumes, challenging the view of Venus as geologically dead.
content:
New Delhi: Venus, long thought to be largely geologically inactive, is back in the spotlight after new analyses suggest some of its crustal rifts are much younger than previously assumed.

A study published in Nature Geoscience on 24 July by researchers at ETH Zurich used advanced 3D thermomechanical computer models to simulate how the Venusian crust responds to internal and atmospheric forcing. The team focused on three major rifts — Ganis Chasma, Dali Chasma and Davana Chasma — and found evidence that these structures may still be active or became inactive only within the last few million years, a very recent interval in geological terms.

The simulations indicate that the crust in these regions was pulled apart at rates of roughly 3–10 cm per year. Such extension is consistent with disruption driven by mantle plumes, columns of hot rock rising from deep inside the planet, which would stretch and thin the crust and create long rift systems. Venusian rifts can run for thousands of kilometers; some are measured nearly 10,000 km in extent, far larger than typical terrestrial analogues such as the African Rift Valley.

"The results help us to better assess the tectonic activity on Venus," said Taras Gerya, Professor of Geodynamics at the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at ETH, in a press release. The finding reinforces a growing view that Venus may host active internal processes despite a surface environment that is hostile and very different from Earth's.

The renewed interest follows earlier work revisiting archival images from NASA's Magellan mission about 30 years ago, where researchers identified features resembling volcanoes. Those discoveries, together with the new modeling, suggest Venus is not necessarily a "dead" planet and that internal heat and tectonic forces may continue to reshape its surface.

Methodologically, the study combined detailed thermomechanical modeling with observations of rift morphology. By coupling crustal behavior with heat and buoyancy effects from underlying mantle plumes, the researchers were able to reproduce patterns of stretching and faulting that match the observed chasmata. The inferred recent activity timescale — millions rather than hundreds of millions of years — has important implications for our understanding of Venusian evolution.

If mantle plumes and ongoing extension are confirmed, they could explain not only the formation of large rift systems but also episodic volcanic activity and localized resurfacing. The authors call for higher-resolution radar mapping and future missions to gather further data on rift structure, composition and any present-day seismic or volcanic activity.

Overall, the study highlights the dynamic potential of Venus's interior and strengthens the case for renewed observational campaigns to resolve lingering questions about the planet's tectonic and volcanic state. Continued modeling, combined with forthcoming missions and improved imagery, will be crucial to determine whether these rifts remain active today or merely record relatively recent geological events.
